title: Understanding coronary heart disease
summary: What CHD is, and the main things that raise your risk.

blocks.text: Coronary heart disease (CHD), also called coronary artery disease, happens when plaque builds up inside the arteries that carry oxygen-rich blood to your heart. Over time this narrows the arteries, so your heart does not get all the blood it needs, especially when it is working harder.

items: High blood pressure
High LDL ("bad") cholesterol
Diabetes
Not being active enough, and carrying extra weight
Smoking
An unhealthy diet
Getting older

Long-term stress

blocks.text: Most of these risk factors can be managed. Small, steady changes - like the ones in the other Learn topics - make a real difference over time.

title: Recognising the signs and symptoms
summary: What angina feels like, and how to tell a warning sign from an emergency.

sections.title: Two ways CHD can show up

blocks.text: Coronary heart disease usually shows up in one of two ways: chronic stable angina, which is predictable chest discomfort brought on by exertion, or acute coronary syndrome (ACS) - a medical emergency that includes unstable angina and heart attack.

items: Quality: often described as pressure, squeezing, fullness, heaviness, or burning - rarely a sharp, stabbing pain
Location: typically felt behind the breastbone
Radiation: may spread to the shoulders, arms (often the left arm), neck, jaw, or back

sections.title: Stable vs. unstable - and other signs

blocks.text: Stable angina happens at predictable times - climbing stairs, emotional stress, a heavy meal - and usually settles within 5 minutes of rest.
Unstable angina is different and dangerous: it can happen at rest, be new, or be more severe and longer-lasting than usual, and it does not go away with rest. Treat it as a medical emergency.

items: Pain or discomfort in one or both arms, the back, neck, jaw, or stomach
Shortness of breath
Cold sweat, nausea, vomiting, or lightheadedness

title: Heart attack warning signs
summary: The signs to know, and what to do if you notice them.

items: Pain or discomfort in the chest, arm, or shoulder
Pain that spreads to the back, neck, or jaw
Shortness of breath
Sweating
Feeling sick or vomiting
Dizziness or feeling lightheaded
Extreme tiredness

blocks.text: Some of these signs - sweating, dizziness, back or jaw pain - are less well known but are common, especially in women. A heart attack does not always feel like the chest-clutching moment shown on TV.
If you notice these signs, tell someone how you feel straight away - do not wait to see if they pass.

Call your emergency contact now if the symptoms are severe, or if they do not improve within about 10 minutes. Every minute matters - the longer it takes to get help, the more the heart muscle can be damaged.

title: Eating well for your heart
summary: A 5-step Ethiopian heart-healthy eating pattern - not a strict diet.

sections.title: It's a pattern, not a restriction

blocks.text: A heart-healthy way of eating is not about cutting everything out. It is a pattern of foods you choose regularly, over time, that is naturally lower in unhealthy fat, salt, and added sugar, and rich in fibre, healthy fats, and protein.

items: 1. Plenty of vegetables, fruit, and whole grains - gomen, ye'abesha gomen, timatim salata, and whole-grain teff injera or kita instead of refined grains
2. A variety of protein-rich foods - shiro, misir, and kik (legumes) most days, with fish, and smaller amounts of eggs and lean meat
3. Milk, yogurt, and cheese - ergo (Ethiopian yogurt) and other dairy in moderation; unflavoured, lower-fat options are the healthiest choice if you have heart disease or high cholesterol
4. Healthy fats and oils - niger seed (nug) oil in place of butter or fatty meat drippings; fish 2-3 times a week if you eat it
5. Flavour with herbs and spices instead of salt - garlic, ginger, koseret, and rue add real flavour without the salt in heavy berbere or added table salt

blocks.text: Too much salt is a real risk factor for high blood pressure. Cutting back on processed and packaged foods, and flavouring meals with herbs and spices instead, is the easiest way to reduce it.

title: Staying physically active
summary: Why moving more helps your heart, and simple ways to do it.

blocks.text: Regular physical activity reduces your risk of a heart attack and helps control common heart disease risk factors, including high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and carrying extra weight. It can also help you feel more energetic, happier, and relaxed.

items: Move more - any activity is better than none
Set realistic goals - start small and build up toward 30-60 minutes of moderate activity most days of the week
Choose activities you enjoy - you're more likely to keep doing them
Get social - being active with friends, family, or even a dog helps you stay motivated
Sit less - people who sit less through the day have a lower risk of early death, especially from heart disease

title: Why your medication matters
summary: Two different jobs your heart medications do, and why taking them as prescribed counts.

sections.title: Two kinds of medicine, two jobs

blocks.text: Heart medications generally do one of two jobs. Some relieve symptoms and improve day-to-day life by easing the heart's workload. Others work silently in the background to prevent future heart attacks, strokes, and worsening disease - you may not feel any different from taking them, but they are still working.

items: Symptom relief: eases chest pain and allows more activity
Disease prevention: protects against future heart attacks and strokes, even without a noticeable day-to-day feeling

sections.title: Why sticking with your plan matters

blocks.text: Prevention medications often work with no symptoms to remind you they're needed. Stopping them because you feel fine can undo their protection - never change or stop a medication without talking to your clinician first.

title: Coping and quitting smoking
summary: How smoking affects your heart, and a real technique for getting through a craving.

blocks.text: Smoking damages the blood vessels leading to your heart, brain, and other parts of your body. It makes you about four times more likely to die of a heart attack or stroke, and three times more likely to die from sudden cardiac death.
The good news: when you quit, your risk of heart attack and stroke starts dropping almost straight away.

sections.title: Getting through a craving: the 5 D's

items: Delay - even for a short while, the urge will pass
Drink water - slowly, and give the craving time to fade
Deep breathing - a few slow breaths can ease the urge
Do something different - change what you're doing or where you are
Discuss the craving - talk it through with someone else

blocks.text: Quitting isn't always easy, and it can take more than one try. Planning, practice, and support all help - and support is available if you're finding it hard.
